title: But Wait, That's Not All
text:
Television salesmen have long used a familiar line: "But wait, there's more!" In 1986 the psychologist Jerry Burger of Santa Clara University tested whether the trick works and why.

At a campus bake sale, a table displayed cupcakes without price tags. When a customer asked about the price, the seller gave one of two answers. In the that's-not-all condition, the seller said the cupcakes cost 75 cents, then, before the customer could respond, added that the price included two cookies. In the control condition, the customer was shown the cupcake and two cookies together from the start and told the package cost 75 cents. The deal was identical. Only the order of presentation differed.

About 73 percent of customers in the that's-not-all condition bought, compared with about 40 percent in the control condition. In another version, the seller first said a cupcake cost one dollar twenty-five, then lowered the price to one dollar before the customer replied, which also sold more than simply asking for one dollar from the start. Burger suggested two forces at work: the improvement felt like a concession that people wanted to return, and the first price served as an anchor that made the final offer look better.
lesson: An offer that improves before you answer feels like a gift, even when it is the same deal. Judge the final offer on its own merits.
location: Santa Clara University, Santa Clara, USA
source: Burger, J. M. (1986). Increasing compliance by improving the deal: The that's-not-all technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 51(2), 277-283.
